description: Second batch of unsent letters written by bunker dwellers to family members they may never see again. Each letter is sealed in the dead-letter pigeonhole system, maintained by Galina the courier.

letters.destination_address: University District, Apartment 7B — last known address
letters.envelope_condition: Standard brown envelope, sealed with electrical tape. A small copper wire is wrapped around the flap like a tie.
letters.letter_text: Anya, I fixed the lights in the mess hall today. The fluorescent tubes were flickering — the ballast was dying. I replaced it with one from the comms room. The mess hall is bright again. The Chef said she could actually see the food she was serving. I thought of you. You were studying electrical engineering. You would have known how to fix the ballast properly. I improvised. I always improvise. That's what electricians do when the supply chain ends. I hope you found shelter. I hope someone is taking care of you. I hope you are not cold. I fixed the lights today. Tomorrow I will fix the water pump. The day after that, I don't know. But I will fix something. It is the only thing I know how to do.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Electrician checks this pigeonhole every Sunday. He never takes the letter out. He just runs his fingers over the envelope like he's reading a braille message only he can feel.

letters.envelope_condition: White envelope sealed with green wax pressed from a crushed leaf. A dried wheat stalk is tucked under the wax seal.
letters.letter_text: Tomas, the wheat from the seed vault germinated today. Seven seeds out of twelve. I know you would have calculated the probability — 58.3 percent, with a standard error based on seed age and storage temperature. You would have been pleased. I am pleased. But I am also frightened. Because if the wheat grows, and if I can get it to seed, and if the soil outside is clean enough to plant it in, then we might have a future. And a future without you is a word I don't know how to spell. I planted the seven seedlings in individual pots. I talk to them. I know that's irrational. They don't care about my voice. But Suki says plants respond to vibration and CO2, so maybe my talking is helping. The third seedling from the left is the strongest. I've named it after you. Don't laugh. It's a wheat plant. It can't laugh either.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Botanist placed a small pot of wheat seedlings beside this pigeonhole on Day 68. She wrote 'For Tomas' on a tag. The seedling in the centre pot is thriving. The others are struggling. She waters all of them equally.

letters.envelope_condition: Brown kraft envelope, sealed with a smear of desk ink. A brass key is taped to the outside — the key to the precinct locker.
letters.letter_text: Dmitri, I found the lockbox. I opened it with the key from the sergeant's desk. Inside was a pistol, two magazines, a box of shells, and a notebook. The notebook has names in it. Some of them I know. Some I don't. The last entry is dated Day 1. It says: 'Sealed the doors. Lost the keys on purpose.' I understand now. The sergeant didn't lose the keys. He threw them away. He wanted the lockbox to be found only by someone who was looking. I was looking. I took the pistol. I took the notebook. I put the key back in the desk. Then I took it out again. Then I threw it in the sump. I don't know what the notebook means. I don't know if the names are people who were saved or people who weren't. I carry the pistol now. Not because I think I'll need it. Because the sergeant thought someone would. I'm trying to be the person he expected.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Cop wrote this letter on the back of a pre-war incident report form. He folded it into quarters and sealed it with ink from a pen that was running dry. The last line is barely legible.

letters.destination_address: Village of Krasnoye, House with the Blue Gate
letters.envelope_condition: Flour-dusted envelope sealed with a paste of water and rye flour. A sprig of dried thyme is tucked inside.
letters.letter_text: Babushka, I made bread today. Real bread. Not the bunker ration paste — actual bread with a crust and a crumb and the smell of a wood-fired oven. I built a hearth from salvaged bricks in the lower corridor. I started a sourdough from dried yeast I found in my coat pocket. You would laugh. You always said I'd forget to eat if I was busy. I didn't forget. I just couldn't cook. Not until now. The bread is not good. It's dense and a little bitter because the flour is made from dried turnips and acorns. But it's bread. It's the thing you made every Sunday morning when I was a child and the kitchen smelled like yeast and warmth and you would give me the heel of the loaf with butter and I would sit on the step and eat it while the cats fought over the crumbs. I saved a piece for you. It's in the envelope. It's probably stale by now. I'm sorry. I'll make another one tomorrow.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Chef baked an extra roll every Sunday and placed it in a wax-paper bag inside this pigeonhole. After two weeks, the pile was six rolls deep. Galina ate one when no one was looking. It tasted like turnips and love.

letters.envelope_condition: Water-stained envelope sealed with candle wax. A hand-drawn weather map is folded inside, showing isobar lines and ash cloud trajectories.
letters.letter_text: Petra, I'm maintaining the weather log. I know no one is reading it. I know the Weather Service probably doesn't exist anymore. But I'm recording the barometric pressure, the wind direction, the temperature, the visibility, and the ash fall rate every six hours. I'm using the bunker's instruments — the ones we salvaged from the observation post. The data is real. The ash storms are predictable. I can forecast them now with about 36 hours of lead time. The pattern is: pressure drops, wind shifts northeast, temperature falls two degrees in six hours, then the storm hits. It's not complicated. It's just consistent. If anyone ever finds this data, they'll know when to seal the hatches. They'll know when to run the filtration on high. They'll know when to stay inside. I'm writing this for them. For the people who come after. The weather doesn't care about the war. Neither do I.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Meteorologist has filled three notebooks with weather data since Day 1. He keeps them in a waterproof bag under his bunk. He copies the summary into this letter every month. No one has ever collected it.

letters.destination_address: Maple Street 22, the house with the garden
letters.envelope_condition: Heavy cream envelope sealed with black wax. No flower, no decoration. The wax is stamped with a plain circle — no symbol.
letters.letter_text: Elena, I have buried thirty-one people in forty days. I know each of their names. I know the weight of a body when you lower it into the ground. I know the sound the earth makes when it hits the coffin lid. I know how long it takes for the flowers to wilt. I didn't know any of this before. Before, I was a carpenter. I made tables and chairs. I sanded things until they were smooth. I varnished them until they shone. Now I dig holes in the frozen ground and put people in them. I don't mind the digging. The cold keeps the bodies. The clay keeps the shape. I can do this. What I can't do is stop knowing their names. I write them down. I say them at the burial. I think about them when I lie down at night. You would tell me to eat something. You always told me to eat when I was upset. There's nothing to eat. So I write this letter instead.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Undertaker wrote this letter in one sitting. The pen pressed so hard it tore the paper in three places. He folded it carefully, sealed it, and placed it in the pigeonhole without looking at Galina. He hasn't checked it since.

letters.intended_recipient: Her Students (Petr, Sonya, Milo, and Anya Jr.)
letters.envelope_condition: Lined notebook paper folded into a square, sealed with a sticker of a gold star — a teacher's reward sticker from a pre-war supply tin.
letters.letter_text: My dear students, I am writing this letter to you even though you are probably sleeping in the dormitory right now. I want you to know some things. Petr: you are the kindest boy I have ever taught. You share your ration with Milo even when you are hungry. That is not weakness. That is the strongest thing a person can do. Sonya: your drawing of the three-legged dog is the best picture in the schoolroom. Keep drawing. The world needs people who can see things as they are and still make them beautiful. Milo: you asked me yesterday if the sun still exists even though we can't see it. Yes, Milo. The sun is still there. It is burning just as it always has. The ash is between us and it. But the sun has not gone out. Anya Jr.: you are the youngest and the bravest. You don't cry when the storms hit. I cry when the storms hit. I just do it where you can't see me. I am your teacher. That means I am supposed to teach you things. But you have taught me more. Stay in school. Keep learning. The world is waiting for you to be ready.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Teacher placed this letter in the schoolroom desk on a Monday morning. By Tuesday, all four children had found it. Sonya drew a picture of a smiling sun and pinned it to the letter. Petr wrote 'Thank you' on the back in very careful letters.

letters.envelope_condition: Military-surplus envelope, olive drab, sealed with duct tape. A spare AA battery is taped to the corner.
letters.letter_text: To whoever finds this: I prepared for the end of the world. I had a bunker. I had food. I had water. I had ammunition. I had a plan. The plan was to survive alone. That was the plan. I was going to outlast everyone and then emerge when it was safe and rebuild by myself. That was the plan. The plan was wrong. You can't survive alone. Not really. You can keep your heart beating and your lungs breathing and your calories above zero. But that's not surviving. That's just not dying yet. The bunker has forty-seven people in it. Some of them are useful. Some of them are not. Some of them are kind and some of them are selfish. All of them are necessary. The Electrician fixes the lights. The Chef makes the food. The Undertaker buries the dead. The Teacher teaches the children. I carry messages between them. That's my job now. Courier. It's not the job I prepared for. It's the job that keeps me alive. If you're reading this, find people. Don't do what I did. Don't prepare to be alone.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Prepper sealed this letter and placed it in the pigeonhole on Day 75. He checked it the next day, took it out, read it, and put it back. He has done this every week since. He has never removed it permanently.

letters.envelope_condition: Lavender-scented envelope sealed with a pressed violet flower under transparent tape. The paper is thin, almost translucent.
letters.letter_text: My darling Katya, I am writing this because I need to tell you something I couldn't say when you were here. Your father did not suffer. I don't know if that's true. He died in the first hour — the blast wave hit the apartment building before the fire reached us. He was instant. The building was not. I was in the kitchen. I survived because the load-bearing wall beside the refrigerator held. The rest of the apartment did not. I crawled out through the bathroom window. I have not been back. I don't know if there is anything left to find. Your father's watch is probably in the rubble. His reading glasses. The book he was reading — some novel about a detective in Prague. I remember he was on page 214. I remember because I marked the page for him when he fell asleep. I am telling you this because you need to know that he was reading. He was doing something ordinary. He was not afraid. He was on page 214 and then he was gone. That is not a tragedy. That is a mercy. I am learning the difference.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The Widow writes a new letter every month. She places the old one back in the envelope and puts the new one in the pigeonhole. Galina has counted fourteen letters in the slot. The Widow has never removed one.

letters.envelope_condition: Military envelope, pre-war stock, sealed with red wax stamped with a simple 'G'. No rank insignia on the envelope.
letters.letter_text: Colonel Voss, I am writing to report that I have failed my mission. My mission was to defend the perimeter. The perimeter is a bunker. The enemy is not at the gate. The enemy is the radiation, the cold, the hunger, the despair, and the slow erosion of the belief that any of this matters. I cannot defend against these things with a rifle. I have spent my life preparing for a war that never came. The war that came was not fought with soldiers. It was fought with megatons and fallout and the collapse of every system I was trained to protect. I am still a soldier. I still wake at 05:00. I still inspect the perimeter. I still maintain the watch rotation. But I am guarding forty-seven civilians from a threat I cannot engage. If you are alive, Colonel, I understand now why you sealed the doors and threw away the keys. The war is over. We lost. The only thing left is to keep the people alive long enough for the ash to settle. That is my new mission. It is not glorious. It is necessary.
letters.galina_dead_letter_note: The General checks this pigeonhole every morning at 05:00, as part of his perimeter inspection route. He has never found a reply. He has never removed the letter. He salutes the pigeonhole on his way back to his bunk.
